claims.text: Pre-applying a thin aluminum-rich layer to boride-based components will improve their resistance to corrosion by molten aluminum.
The aluminum-rich layer will form a protective alumina barrier in situ.
Pack cementation can deposit a thin, uniform aluminum-rich coating on the boride-based components.
Standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions involve high-temperature exposure to molten aluminum in an oxidizing atmosphere.
The aluminized surface will oxidize during initial exposure.
Initial oxidation will produce a continuous, adherent Al2O3 film.
The Al2O3 film will act as a diffusion barrier at the component surface.
The pre-deposited aluminum layer will react with ambient or residual oxygen to generate a stable alumina scale.
The alumina scale will limit direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Limiting contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate will reduce aluminum infiltration and chemical attack.
Aluminum infiltration and chemical attack are typical corrosion processes for boride-based components exposed to molten aluminum.
Aluminized components will exhibit a lower corrosion rate than untreated boride-based components under identical exposure conditions.
Aluminized components will retain better microstructural integrity than untreated components.
The corrosion-resistance benefit will persist while the alumina layer remains protective at the operating temperature.
Extreme thermal cycling or mechanical stress can disrupt the alumina scale and diminish its corrosion-resistance benefit.
